text: Real analysis rarely lives in one table. Orders are in one place, customer details in another, and monthly files arrive separately. pandas gives you merge for joining side by side, and concat for stacking. You already know join types from T-SQL, so here we focus on the pandas syntax and its pitfalls.

Merge takes the key with on, and the join type with how. Inner, left, right, outer: same names, same meaning as SQL. The default is inner, so only rows matching on both sides survive. In our illustrative data, a sixth customer with no orders simply vanishes from an inner join.

Switch to a left join from customers and that sixth customer stays, with missing values in the order columns. Better still, add indicator equals True. pandas creates an underscore merge column saying both, left only or right only. Filter on left only and you have an anti-join, a great way to audit any join.

Now the silent killer. If the key is duplicated on the lookup side, each match repeats. Suppose one customer appears twice in the customers table. Merging orders onto it returns ten rows instead of eight, and no error. Totals inflate quietly. Add validate equals many-to-one and pandas raises a MergeError instead.

Concat stacks tables that share columns, like UNION ALL. Each piece keeps its own index labels, so stacking can produce duplicates like zero, one, two, zero. Pass ignore index equals True to renumber. If columns differ, concat keeps them all and fills gaps with NaN, so check for typos in column names.
Always compare row counts before and after a merge. Next up: reshaping tables with pivot and melt.
